planting.note: Plant huli or corm sections once soil has warmed; traditionally raised as an upland taro in evenly moist, well-drained beds rather than a flooded lo'i.

directions: Pa'akala is one of the named Hawaiian upland poi taro varieties documented in historical surveys of island taro culture, grown in dryland beds rather than permanently flooded patches. Give it rich, humus-heavy soil that is kept constantly damp but not waterlogged, with light overhead shade during the hottest part of the day. Corms are ready to dig roughly 9 to 12 months after planting, and like all taro, corms and leaves must be thoroughly cooked to neutralize calcium oxalate before eating. It makes a reasonable container or bog-margin crop outside the tropics where winters stay frost-free.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Pa'akala)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)

planting.note: Grows best in a permanently saturated or shallowly flooded bed that mimics a traditional wetland lo'i.

directions: Pi'iali'i is a traditionally wetland-grown Hawaiian taro variety recorded among the named poi taro of the islands, recognized by its reddish-tinged petioles against broad green leaves. Keep the root zone continuously wet or shallowly flooded through the growing season for best corm size, and provide part-day shade in hot climates to protect foliage from scorching. Corms generally need 10 to 14 months to size up before harvest, and both corms and greens require thorough cooking before eating to break down irritating calcium oxalate. A pond-edge planter or heavily mulched bog bed works well as a substitute for a true lo'i.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Pi'iali'i)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)

planting.note: Adaptable to either flooded wetland culture or consistently moist upland beds, depending on local water availability.

directions: Moi (literally 'king' in Hawaiian) is one of the old named Hawaiian taro varieties recorded in island agricultural surveys, grown historically in both wetland and upland settings. Maintain even, heavy moisture throughout the growing season and give it part-day shade in warm climates to keep the broad leaves from scorching. Expect corms to reach harvestable size roughly 9 to 12 months after planting corm pieces or huli. As with all taro, cook the corm and leaves thoroughly before eating to eliminate the calcium oxalate crystals that cause throat and skin irritation when raw.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Moi)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)

planting.note: Set huli in evenly moist, well-drained upland beds rather than a flooded patch; this variety is traditionally grown as dryland taro.

directions: Mana Ulu belongs to the large 'mana' group of named Hawaiian upland taro varieties recorded in historical island surveys, grown for a fast, reliable dryland crop rather than for flooded lo'i culture. Keep soil consistently damp but well drained, since this variety does not tolerate standing water as well as the wetland types, and site it with some afternoon shade in hot climates. Corms can be ready for harvest in as little as 8 to 11 months, making it one of the quicker-maturing named Hawaiian taro selections. Cook corms and leaves thoroughly before eating, as with all taro, to break down calcium oxalate.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Mana Ulu)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)

planting.note: Grow in evenly moist upland rows with light overhead shade; tolerates garden culture better than strictly wetland taro types.

directions: Elepaio is a named upland Hawaiian taro variety recorded in historical taro surveys, taking its name from the small speckle-marked native Hawaiian forest bird. Keep the bed consistently moist and provide part-day shade in hot climates to prevent the large leaves from scorching. Corms generally take 9 to 12 months to reach full size, and it adapts reasonably well to a shaded, well-mulched garden row outside the tropics. Cook corms and greens thoroughly before eating to neutralize the calcium oxalate present in raw taro.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Elepaio)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)

planting.note: Best grown in a permanently flooded or saturated bed resembling a traditional wetland lo'i; the long smooth leaves are the signature trait of this variety.

directions: Lauloa Palakea takes its name from its unusually long, smooth-margined leaves ('lauloa' meaning long leaf, 'palakea' meaning smooth), and is among the named wetland poi taro varieties recorded in historical Hawaiian agricultural surveys. Keep it in continuously saturated or shallowly flooded soil through the growing season, with part-day shade to protect the foliage in hot climates. Corms typically need 10 to 14 months of steady moisture before they are ready to dig. Cook corms and leaves thoroughly before eating, as with all Colocasia esculenta, to break down calcium oxalate crystals.
sources: University of Hawaii CTAHR, Taro Varieties in Hawaii database (Lauloa Palakea)
Whitney, Bowers & Takahashi, Taro Varieties in Hawaii, University of Hawaii Agricultural Experiment Station Bulletin 84 (1939)
